name: โปรตีนในปัสสาวะ
preview_text: ในการแพทย์แผนจีน โปรตีนในปัสสาวะไม่ได้เป็นเพียงปัญหาเกี่ยวกับไตเท่านั้น แต่ยังมักเป็นเรื่องราวของม้ามล้มเหลวในการจัดการของเหลว และไตสูญเสียความสามารถในการควบคุมสารสำคัญ ด้วยสมุนไพรเฉพาะทาง...
categories: ["ปัญหาทางเดินปัสสาวะและกระเพาะปัสสาวะ", "ภาวะไต"]
synonyms: ["Albuminuria", "Excess Protein In Urine", "Excessive Urine Protein", "High Levels Of Albumin In Urine", "Kidney Disease With Proteinuria", "Protein In The Urine", "Protein In Urine"]
conventional_description:
Proteinuria is the medical term for excess protein in the urine. Normally, the kidneys filter waste while keeping proteins and other important substances in the blood. When the kidney's filtering units (glomeruli) are damaged, protein can leak through, often indicating an underlying condition such as diabetes, high blood pressure, glomerulonephritis, or autoimmune diseases.
It's usually detected through a simple urine dipstick test or a more precise 24-hour urine collection. Mild, temporary proteinuria can occur after intense exercise or during illness, but persistent proteinuria is a red flag that requires investigation. Conventional treatment focuses on managing the root cause, such as controlling blood sugar and blood pressure, and using medications that reduce pressure inside the glomeruli to slow the leakage.
conventional_treatments: Standard Western treatment includes angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) to lower intraglomerular pressure and reduce protein excretion. For diabetic patients, SGLT2 inhibitors are also used. Dietary modifications, such as reducing salt and protein intake, are recommended. If an autoimmune disease is the cause, immunosuppressive drugs may be prescribed. The goal is to slow kidney damage and prevent progression to chronic kidney disease.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, protein is considered a form of 'essence' (Jīng), a precious substance stored by the Kidneys and nourished by the Spleen's transformation of food. When protein appears in the urine, it's a sign that the body is failing to hold onto its essence. This failure is rarely due to one single cause; instead, it's often a combination of weakened holding power (Spleen and Kidney deficiency) and disruptive factors like Dampness, Heat, or Blood Stasis that disturb the kidneys' filtering function.
The Spleen is responsible for managing fluids and keeping substances in their proper place. If Spleen Qi is weak, Dampness accumulates, creating a heavy, turbid environment that overwhelms the Kidneys. The Kidneys, in turn, govern the body's fundamental Yang and Yin energies. When Kidney Yang is deficient, there isn't enough warmth to transform fluids and secure essence; when Kidney Yin is depleted, the cooling anchor fails, and deficiency heat further opens the gates, allowing protein to escape. Mixed patterns, such as Qi and Yin Deficiency, are also common in chronic conditions.
This is why two people with the same lab result can feel completely different: one may be cold, swollen, and exhausted (Kidney Yang Deficiency), while another may feel hot, dry, and restless (Kidney Yin Deficiency), and yet another may have burning urination and a heavy sensation (Damp-Heat). TCM treatment is tailored to the specific pattern, not just the symptom, which is why it can improve both the proteinuria and the person's overall vitality.
classical_quote: 「虚劳小便白浊，此由劳伤于肾，肾气虚冷故也。肾主水，而开窍于二阴，肾气虚冷，不能制于津液，则使小便白浊。」
classical_translation: "In consumptive disease, white turbid urine occurs because of taxation damage to the Kidneys, resulting in Kidney Qi deficiency and cold. The Kidneys govern water and open into the two lower orifices; when Kidney Qi is deficient and cold, it cannot control the body fluids, leading to white turbid urine."
classical_source:
《诸病源候论》 (Zhu Bing Yuan Hou Lun, Treatise on the Origins and Symptoms of Diseases)  ,  卷四·虚劳小便白浊候 (Volume 4, Section: White Turbid Urine due to Consumptive Disease) 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking about your energy levels, urination habits, and any discomfort or swelling. The quality of the proteinuria - whether it appears alongside fatigue, coldness, or urinary irritation - gives the first clues. The tongue and pulse are then examined to confirm which pattern is at play.
If you feel chronically tired, have a poor appetite, loose stools, and a heavy sensation in the limbs, Spleen Deficiency with Dampness is likely. The tongue will appear pale with a greasy white coating, and the pulse will feel soft or slippery. This reflects the spleen’s failure to manage fluids, allowing dampness to build up and protein to leak.
When cold intolerance, sore and weak lower back and knees, and frequent nighttime urination are prominent, Kidney Yang Deficiency is suspected. The tongue looks pale and swollen with a white coating, and the pulse is deep, slow, and weak. The warming power of Kidney Yang is too low to hold essence, so protein escapes, often with noticeable edema.
A person who complains of dry mouth and throat, hot palms and soles, night sweats, and restlessness may have Kidney Yin Deficiency. The tongue is red with little or no coating, and the pulse is thin and rapid. Here, deficient Yin fails to anchor the kidney’s storing function, and deficiency heat disturbs the gate, causing protein loss.
Qi and Yin Deficiency often arises in chronic conditions. You might feel weak and easily fatigued (Qi deficiency) yet also have dry mouth, thirst, and mild heat sensations (Yin deficiency). The tongue may be pale or red with a thin, dry coating, and the pulse is weak and thready. This dual weakness leaves the body unable to secure essential substances.
If your urine is dark yellow, burning, and frequent, with a heavy sensation in the lower abdomen, Damp-Heat in the Lower Burner is the culprit. The tongue is red with a yellow greasy coating, and the pulse is rapid and slippery. Heat and dampness disrupt the kidney and bladder’s filtering ability, allowing protein to spill into the urine.
When there is fixed, stabbing pain in the lower back or flanks and the urine may contain blood, Blood Stagnation is considered. The tongue shows purple spots or a dusky color, and the pulse is choppy or wiry. Chronic illness leads to stasis that blocks the kidney collaterals, preventing proper storage of essence and causing leakage.

patterns.symptoms: ["Foamy or frothy urine", "Loose stools or diarrhoea", "Abdominal bloating, worse after eating", "Feeling of heaviness in the body and limbs", "Fatigue and lack of energy", "Sticky or greasy sensation in the mouth"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold, raw, or greasy foods, Damp or humid weather, Overeating or irregular meals, Mental overwork and fatigue
patterns.better_with: Warm, cooked meals, Rest and moderate activity, Dry, warm environment, Gentle exercise like walking
patterns.why_this_happens: The Spleen is responsible for transforming food into Qi and managing body fluids. When Spleen Qi is weak, it fails to do this properly, leading to an accumulation of Dampness. This Dampness overwhelms the Kidneys' ability to store and retain the body's essential substances, and protein-a precious essence-leaks into the urine, making it appear frothy. The result is the combination of digestive symptoms like bloating and loose stools with foamy urine.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with teeth marks, and a white greasy coating that looks moist. Pulse: soggy (Ru) and slowed-down (Huan), often soft and lacking force.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold, raw, and greasy foods are difficult for a weak Spleen to transform, and they directly generate more Dampness. Overeating and irregular meals overwhelm the digestive system. Damp weather adds external Dampness that the body must fight. Rest and warm meals conserve Spleen Qi and support its function, while light movement keeps Qi flowing so Dampness does not stagnate. A dry environment helps the body shed excess moisture.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked, easily digestible foods like congee, soups, and steamed vegetables. Avoid cold, raw, greasy, and sweet foods that create Dampness. Gentle daily exercise like walking helps move Qi and dry Dampness. Keep the living environment dry and avoid damp basements.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Dampness and Heat combine, they tend to sink to the Lower Burner, where they invade the bladder and kidneys. This hot, sticky mixture disrupts the kidney's ability to store essence and the bladder's role in separating clear from turbid. Essential proteins that should be retained are instead leaked into the urine, producing proteinuria with dark, yellow, and often painful urination.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, yellow greasy coating thickest at the root, slightly swollen. Pulse: slippery (Hua) and rapid (Shu), often soggy (Ru), more pronounced at the Chi (rear) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spicy, greasy, and alcoholic foods directly generate Dampness and Heat in the body, fueling the pathogenic factors that pour down to the Lower Burner. Hot, humid environments further aggravate the Damp-Heat. Cooling, bland foods and adequate hydration help to dilute and flush out the Damp-Heat, while rest prevents the body from generating more internal heat. Emotional upset, especially anger, can stir up Liver Fire, which combines with Dampness and worsens the condition.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol and excessive sweet drinks, which generate dampness and heat. Eat cooling, diuretic foods like watermelon, cucumber, celery, and mung beans. Maintain good hygiene in the genital area to prevent external dampness from invading. Stay in a dry environment and avoid prolonged sitting on damp surfaces.

faqs.question: Can Chinese medicine really reduce protein in my urine?
faqs.answer: Yes, many patients see a measurable decrease in urine protein levels with consistent TCM treatment. Clinical studies and centuries of practice show that herbal formulas and acupuncture can strengthen the Spleen and Kidneys, reduce Dampness, and help the body retain its essential proteins. However, results depend on the underlying pattern and the severity of kidney damage; it's important to continue regular medical monitoring alongside TCM care.

faqs.question: How long before I notice a difference?
faqs.answer: Many people feel an improvement in energy, digestion, and swelling within the first few weeks. A reduction in urine protein levels usually takes longer - often 2-3 months for the first measurable change, with continued improvement over 6 months or more. Deficiency patterns take more time because the body needs to rebuild its reserves, not just clear a temporary imbalance.

faqs.question: Can I take Chinese herbs with my blood pressure or diabetes medication?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes, but it's essential that both your TCM practitioner and your medical doctor know exactly what you're taking. Some herbs can influence blood pressure or fluid balance, so your dosages may need adjustment. Never stop or reduce your prescribed medications on your own - TCM is used as a complement, not a replacement, especially in serious kidney conditions.

faqs.question: What dietary changes should I make?
faqs.answer: In general, TCM recommends eating warm, cooked foods that are easy to digest, like soups, stews, and congee. Avoid raw, cold, greasy, and heavily processed foods that burden the Spleen. Reducing salt is also important to manage fluid retention. Specific foods like Chinese yam (Shān Yào), lotus seeds, and Job's tears can support the Spleen and Kidneys; your practitioner will tailor advice to your pattern.

faqs.question: Is acupuncture safe if I have kidney disease?
faqs.answer: Yes, acupuncture is generally safe and can be very helpful for managing symptoms like fatigue, back pain, and edema. The points chosen are away from the kidneys themselves and focus on balancing the body's energy. Always inform your acupuncturist about your kidney condition and any blood-thinning medications you may be taking.

faqs.question: Will the proteinuria come back after I stop treatment?
faqs.answer: If the underlying imbalance hasn't been fully corrected, proteinuria can return. That's why TCM treatment often continues for a period after lab results improve, to consolidate the gains and strengthen the body's foundation. Many patients transition to a maintenance phase with occasional treatments and dietary care to prevent recurrence.

faqs.question: Can TCM help if my proteinuria is caused by an autoimmune disease?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can address the underlying immune dysregulation by harmonizing the body's Qi and clearing pathogenic factors like Heat and Dampness. While it does not replace immunosuppressive therapy, it may help reduce the frequency of flare-ups and improve overall resilience. Work closely with your rheumatologist and TCM practitioner to coordinate care.

research.title: 2 例阿帕替尼致蛋白尿的中医辨证治疗
research.description: A case report of two patients who developed proteinuria as a side effect of the cancer drug apatinib. TCM differentiation-based treatment with spleen-tonifying and kidney-securing herbs led to a marked reduction in urine protein, demonstrating TCM's potential for managing drug-induced renal injury.
research.periodical: Authors not specified. 皖南医学院学报 (Journal of Wannan Medical College). 2022.

research.title: 中西医结合处理糖尿病肾病蛋白尿的研究进展
research.description: A narrative review summarizing the mechanisms and clinical evidence for integrated Chinese-Western treatment of proteinuria in diabetic kidney disease, highlighting the roles of Shen Ling Bai Zhu San, Jin Gui Shen Qi Wan, and other classical formulas in reducing protein leakage and preserving renal function.
research.periodical: Authors not specified. 临床与病理杂志 (Journal of Clinical and Pathological Research). 2025.
